paragraphs.heading: The first person in space
paragraphs.text: Yuri Gagarin was a Soviet pilot and cosmonaut, and he was the first person ever to travel into outer space. On 12 April 1961 he rode the Vostok 1 spacecraft up from the Baikonur Cosmodrome, in what was then the Kazakh SSR, and went once around Earth. It was the first crewed spaceflight to succeed. He lived from 9 March 1934 to 27 March 1968.

paragraphs.heading: A village at war
paragraphs.text: Gagarin was born in Klushino, a village in the Russian SFSR near the town of Gzhatsk. His parents worked on a farm, his father as a carpenter and his mother as a dairy farmer, and Yuri was the third of four children. German forces captured the village on 18 October 1941, during the Second World War. On their first day they burned the school, which ended Yuri's first year of lessons. A Nazi officer took over the family home, and the Gagarins spent 21 months in a mud hut about 3 by 3 metres on the land behind it.

paragraphs.heading: Small acts of resistance
paragraphs.text: Yuri fought back in small ways. After a German soldier tried to hang his younger brother Boris from an apple tree, Yuri spoiled that soldier's work by pouring soil into tank batteries waiting to be recharged and mixing up the chemicals meant for the job. In early 1943 the Germans sent his two older siblings to Poland as forced labourers. They escaped, but they did not come home until 1945, after the war, and the rest of the family had believed they were dead.

paragraphs.heading: School, work and flying
paragraphs.text: In 1946 the family moved to Gzhatsk, where Yuri carried on with school; he learned to read from a discarded army manual, and maths and science were his favourite subjects. He had loved aircraft since he was small, and a Yakovlev fighter that crash-landed in Klushino during the war fed that interest. At 16 he started as an apprentice foundryman at a steel plant in Lyubertsy, near Moscow. Later, while studying tractors at a technical school in Saratov, he trained at a flying club on weekends, first in a biplane and then in a Yak-18.

paragraphs.heading: From pilot to cosmonaut
paragraphs.text: In 1955 he was accepted into an air force pilots' school in Orenburg. He went on to serve as a pilot in the Soviet Air Forces at Luostari Air Base, close to the border with Norway. From there he was picked for the Soviet space programme along with five other cosmonauts.

paragraphs.heading: After Vostok 1
paragraphs.text: Vostok 1 was the only time Gagarin went to space. Afterward he became the deputy head of training at the centre where cosmonauts trained, a centre that now bears his name, and he was elected to both chambers of the Supreme Soviet. He was the backup for Soyuz 1, a flight that ended in a fatal crash that killed his friend Vladimir Komarov. Soviet officials, afraid of losing a national hero, banned him from any further spaceflights.

paragraphs.heading: An early death
paragraphs.text: In February 1968 he finished training at the Zhukovsky Air Force Engineering Academy and was allowed to fly ordinary aircraft again. Five weeks later he was killed when the MiG-15 he was piloting with instructor Vladimir Seryogin crashed near the town of Kirzhach. After his death that year, Gzhatsk, the town where his family had moved in 1946, was renamed Gagarin.
